final_proof:
Fix a finite population U of N people and a partition of U into nonempty families. The standard precise interpretation of the probabilistic assumptions is that, after the family partition and hence all family sizes have been fixed, each person is independently declared male or female, with probability 1/2 of each. Thus “half are men and half are women” means half in expectation (and approximately half in a large population). Choose a person I uniformly from U, independently of the sex assignments. We prove that the two conditional expectations in the question are equal.

For u in U, write F(u) for u's family, n(u)=|F(u)|, and X_u=1 if u is male and X_u=0 if u is female. The number of brothers of u is

B_u = sum over v in F(u), v != u, of X_v.

Because P(X_u=s)=1/2 for every u and s in {0,1},

P(I=u | X_I=s) = P(I=u and X_u=s)/P(X_I=s) = ((1/N)(1/2))/(1/2) = 1/N.

Moreover, independence of the sex assignments gives, for either s=0 or s=1,

E(B_u | X_u=s) = sum over v in F(u), v != u, of P(X_v=1 | X_u=s) = (n(u)-1)/2.

Consequently,

E(B_I | X_I=s) = (1/N) sum over u in U of (n(u)-1)/2
                 = (1/(2N)) sum over families A of |A|(|A|-1),

which does not depend on s. Hence

E(number of brothers of I | I is female) = E(number of brothers of I | I is male).

No distribution of family sizes was used: the equality holds conditional on every fixed list of family sizes.

Here is the precise flaw in the proposed contrary argument. In a realized family containing b boys and g girls, each girl has b brothers whereas each boy has b-1 brothers. That comparison is correct after the complete sex composition of the family has been fixed. It cannot simply be averaged over families, however, because conditioning the sampled person to be male or female changes which realized compositions are likely to contain that person. Conditional on a focal person being female in a family of size n, the number of boys among the other n-1 members is Binomial(n-1,1/2), and all of them are her brothers. Conditional on the focal person being male, the total number of boys is 1+Binomial(n-1,1/2), but the focal boy is not his own brother, so his number of brothers is again Binomial(n-1,1/2). The apparent extra brother of a girl is exactly offset by the fact that, in the male-conditioned case, one of the boys is the focal person himself.

One can also see why the family-by-family averaging inference is invalid without probability. Consider two families, one with 100 boys and 1 girl and the other with 1 boy and 100 girls. Within each family a girl has one more brother than a boy, yet across the whole population the 101 women have 200 brother-incidences in total, while the 101 men have 9900 brother-incidences in total. Thus the men have far more brothers on average in that realized population. Conversely, if every family consists of one boy and one girl, women average one brother and men average zero. A statement true under comparison within every family therefore need not determine the comparison of the two differently weighted population averages.

Finally, if “exactly half” is intended as a hard constraint rather than as a fair independent model, it must be treated separately. In the natural exact-total model, N is even and the N/2 male labels are chosen uniformly without replacement. The labels are then not independent. Put D=(1/N) sum over u of (n(u)-1). Given that a focal person is female, each other person has conditional probability (N/2)/(N-1) of being male; given that the focal person is male, each other person has probability (N/2-1)/(N-1) of being male. Therefore

E(B_I | I female) = D (N/2)/(N-1),
E(B_I | I male)   = D (N/2-1)/(N-1).

The female expectation exceeds the male expectation by D/(N-1), unless D=0. This is a small finite-population effect caused precisely by abandoning independence and imposing an exact total. Thus under the independent-sex assumption the rigorous answer is equality; under uniform assignment with an exactly fixed 50-50 total, women have the displayed slight advantage.
